[edit | edit source]
The origins of the Ukrainian College date back to the 16th century and were at first closely linked with the Greek Pontifical College of Saint Athanasius, which was founded in 1576. That college was not only attended by Greek and Greek-speaking seminarians but also by Ukrainians until 1897, except for the period between 1803 and 1845, when the Greek College was closed.
On 18 December 1897 Pope Leo XIII approved the foundation of a separate Ukrainian college and in 1904 the Basilian Order of St Josaphat/Order of Saint Basil the Great (who also had the General Curia in Rome, Italy) transferred into the college. It was first sited on Piazza Madonna dei Monti, but on 13 November 1932 a new building was opened for it on the Janiculum Hill. It now has between 20 and 50 students and its rector is Father Genesio Viomar OSBM.

value.text:
The Ukrainian Pontifical College of Saint Josaphat is a specialist seminary and pontifical college in Rome, Italy, serving seminarians and priests of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church. Its patron saint is Josaphat Kuntsevych. The college includes the church of San Giosafat al Gianicolo, one of Ukraine’s national churches in Rome. Its historical roots are connected with the Greek Pontifical College of Saint Athanasius, founded in 1576. Ukrainian seminarians attended that institution until 1897, apart from its closure between 1803 and 1845. This earlier educational connection is distinct from the establishment of the separate Ukrainian college.

On 18 December 1897, Pope Leo XIII approved the foundation of that separate college. In 1904 the Basilian Order of St Josaphat, also known as the Order of Saint Basil the Great, transferred into it. Initially located on Piazza Madonna dei Monti, the college received a new building on Janiculum Hill, opened on 13 November 1932. Sofron Stefan Mudry served as rector from 1974 to 1994. The college’s academic and religious role centers on its Ukrainian Greek Catholic seminarians and priests; an undated account reports between 20 and 50 students.
